what.heading: What is a dictionary?
paragraphs: A dictionary stores values under labels called **keys**, inside curly braces `{ }`. It's a good fit for what you find in a document: its type, its vendor, its dates.

points.title: Nested
points.text: A value can be another dictionary: `record["dates"]["issue"]`.

points.title: Many records
points.text: A list of dictionaries holds one record per document. `pd.DataFrame()` shows it as a table.

example.heading: What it looks like
example.caption: `record["dates"]` is a dictionary of its own, so `record["dates"]["issue"]` goes one level deeper and gives "2024-03-15". This record is made up.

demos.label: Read a value
demos.code:
record = {"doc_type": "Certificate of Quality", "vendor": "Example Bio Supplies"}
print(record["vendor"])
print(record.get("lot_number"))
print(record.get("lot_number", "not found"))
demos.note: Square brackets read a key. .get() does the same, but gives None (or a default you choose) when the key is missing, instead of a KeyError.

demos.label: Add or change a key
demos.code:
record = {"doc_type": "Certificate of Quality"}
record["lot_number"] = "AB-4417"
record["doc_type"] = "Material Description"
print(record)
demos.note: Assigning to a new key adds it. Assigning to a key that exists replaces its value.

demos.label: Nested dictionary
demos.code:
record = {
    "doc_type": "BSE/TSE Declaration",
    "dates": {"issue": "2023-06-01", "expiry": "2026-06-01"},
}
dates = record["dates"]
print(dates)
print(dates["expiry"])
demos.note: Read the outer key first, then the inner key.

demos.label: List of dicts as a table
demos.code:
import pandas as pd

records = [
    {"doc_type": "Cover Letter", "vendor": "Example Bio Supplies", "issue_date": "2025-01-10"},
    {"doc_type": "Certificate of Quality", "vendor": "Sample Vials Co.", "issue_date": "2024-03-15"},
    {"doc_type": "Chain of Custody", "vendor": "Demo Filters Ltd.", "issue_date": "2022-08-30"},
]
df = pd.DataFrame(records)
print(df)
demos.note: Each dictionary becomes a row, and each key becomes a column. In Colab, put df on the last line of a cell instead of print(df) to see a formatted table.

try.prompt: Add a third record to `records`: a **Chain of Custody** from "Demo Filters Ltd.", issued "2022-08-30". Use the same three keys. Then build `df` from `records` with `pd.DataFrame()`.
try.starter:
import pandas as pd

records = [
    {"doc_type": "Cover Letter", "vendor": "Example Bio Supplies", "issue_date": "2025-01-10"},
    {"doc_type": "Certificate of Quality", "vendor": "Sample Vials Co.", "issue_date": "2024-03-15"},
]
# 1. append the Chain of Custody record
# 2. make df from records
try.solution:
import pandas as pd

records = [
    {"doc_type": "Cover Letter", "vendor": "Example Bio Supplies", "issue_date": "2025-01-10"},
    {"doc_type": "Certificate of Quality", "vendor": "Sample Vials Co.", "issue_date": "2024-03-15"},
]
records.append({"doc_type": "Chain of Custody", "vendor": "Demo Filters Ltd.", "issue_date": "2022-08-30"})
df = pd.DataFrame(records)
print(df)

checks.hint: .append() changes the list in place and gives back None. Write records.append(...) on its own line, not records = records.append(...).
records should hold 3 dictionaries. Add the new one to the end with records.append({...}).
The new record should be a dictionary whose "doc_type" key holds "Chain of Custody". Check the curly braces, the key name and the spelling.
The new record needs "vendor": "Demo Filters Ltd." and "issue_date": "2022-08-30", with the same key names as the other two records.
Make the table with df = pd.DataFrame(records).
df should have 3 rows and 3 columns, with Demo Filters Ltd. in the last row. Build df after you append the new record, so it includes it.
